To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have developed a menu of new measures to assess how large-scale social change and other macro-level factors affect the HIV epidemic, and that we have found preliminary evidence of their validity.

(a) we have developed a menu of measures to assess hypothesized pathways between macro-social changes and HIV transmission; and (b) these measures show some evidence of reliability and criterion validity.

we developed a set of measures to assess how large-scale social changes and structural interventions might influence HIV transmission by changing contexts of risk, and that these measures show evidence of criterion validity and reliability.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how social change affects the spread of HIV.
the effects on health of macro-social change.
the effects of social change on sexual and drug injection risk, and on HIV transmission.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
these measures have been shown to be promising, not that they are ready for use in all settings.
these measures are promising but need further testing.
these measures show promise for use in research on structural and social determinants of HIV risk.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the new measures have promise, but that they are not yet ready for prime time.
these new measures can provide a basis for understanding the links between large-scale social changes and HIV risk behaviors and infection.
we have developed a menu of new scales that can be used to understand links between large-scale social changes and subsequent risk behaviors and HIV transmission.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to develop new measures of constructs that can be studied in the context of large-scale social change.
there is no single “best” measure for any construct; the best measure depends on what is needed.
it is possible to develop measures that assess the impact of macro-social change on risk and that can be used in studies of risk and transmission in more ordinary circumstances.
